SOURCE: "MiniMax Sparse Attention" (MSA). Xunhao Lai, Weiqi Xu, ... Pengyu Zhao (MiniMax, Peking Univ., NVIDIA and others). arXiv:2606.13392v2 [cs.AI], 12 Jun 2026; the footer reads "©2026 MiniMax". Preprint, no venue. Kernel: github.com/MiniMax-AI/MSA. Model: huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3.

COVERAGE: 87,294 of 87,294 chars read (main text, appendices A-C, ablation tables). References were skimmed. Figure content (plots) was not viewed. Only the text captions and the numbers printed on the plot axes came through.

KEY WARNING FOR "Shrinking the cache": MSA does NOT shrink the KV cache. It cuts attention compute and the KV reads per token. The paper reports no KV-memory figure at all. The selector picks blocks from a full cache that is still stored. I found no KV-memory claim, no cache-size figure and no cache-eviction mechanism. It does not mention the added index-key cache either. If the note's section is about cache size, MSA belongs as a contrast case: reduce bytes read per decode step, not bytes stored. This contrast is my inference. The paper does not state it. It does contrast MSA with H2O and SnapKV, which "prune the KV cache during decoding" (p.13).

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: At 1M context MSA cuts per-token attention FLOPs 28.4x versus dense GQA.
  number: 28.4x
  setup: 64 query heads, 4 KV heads, head dim 128, Bk=128, k=16 (2,048 tokens per query). The FLOPs figure is analytic, from Eq. 12.
  quote: "At 1M tokens, the FLOPs reduction reaches 28.4× under the same head configuration."
  where: Sec 5.4, p.12; Fig 4 left
- claim: Measured attention-kernel speedup at 1M is 14.2x for prefill and 7.6x for decode on H800.
  number: 14.2x prefill, 7.6x decode
  setup: same head config as above. The comparison is GQA attention against MSA attention latency at 1M tokens, not end-to-end model latency. The paper says "H800" only in the abstract. Fig 4 axes: prefill latency up to about 30 s, decode up to about 0.9 ms. The Fig 4 labels say "speedup at 1M tokens". Batch size and precision are not given for these.
  quote: "MSAachieves14 .2× prefill and7.6× decoding wall-clock speedups on H800."
  where: abstract, p.1; Fig 4 middle and right, p.12
- claim: The speedup is below the FLOPs reduction because of overheads, and it grows with context length.
  number: none
  quote: "the runtime speedup is smaller than the theoretical FLOPs reduction, but it increases with context length as the dense baseline continues to scale with the full sequence whileMSAkeeps the main attention budget fixed."
  where: Sec 5.4, p.12
- claim: Each query attends to a fixed budget of 2,048 KV tokens (16 blocks of 128), so per-query attention cost is O(kBk), independent of N.
  number: 2,048 tokens
  quote: "Since each query and GQA group still attends to only𝑘𝐵𝑘 = 16× 128 = 2,048key-value tokens"
  where: Sec 5.3, p.11. Complexity in Sec 3.1 and Eq. 12.
- claim: Quality is on par with full-attention GQA at 109B MoE scale.
  number: see rows below
  setup: 41-layer MoE, about 109B total and 6B active parameters, d_model 3072, 64 Q heads, 4 KV heads, 3T training tokens, natively multimodal. MSA-PT (from scratch, 40B-token indexer warmup) and MSA-CPT (from a 2.6T-token GQA checkpoint, then 400B tokens of CPT, the first 40B being warmup). Table 2, Full / MSA-PT / MSA-CPT:
  - MMLU 67.0 / 67.2 / 66.8
  - GSM8K 76.2 / 77.7 / 73.7
  - HumanEval 61.0 / 64.0 / 57.9
  - BBH 67.7 / 66.6 / 66.1
  - RULER-8K 79.8 / 84.2 / 77.2
  - RULER-32K 75.0 / 77.5 / 75.7
  - ChartQA 75.0 / 75.4 / 71.4
  - MMMU 46.8 / 45.9 / 44.5
  - EgoSchema 29.6 / 37.6 / 25.8
  - PPL TAU2 1.155 / 1.148 / 1.150
  quote: "Both sparse models remain broadly competitive with the Full-Attention baseline, indicating that replacing dense attention withMSAdoes not substantially degrade the model’s general language, reasoning, multimodal, or agent-oriented perplexity profile."
  where: Sec 5.3, p.10-11, Table 2
- claim: Training is as stable as full attention. The LM-loss curves are nearly indistinguishable over 3T tokens (final 50B-token window about 1.21-1.22).
  number: 3T tokens
  quote: "training a sparse attention model is as stable as training the full-attention baseline at a large scale."
  where: Sec 5.2, p.9; Fig 2
- claim: After about 140B tokens of long-context extension, MSA-CPT stays close to full attention at 128K.
  number: HELMET-128K overall 46.53 vs 45.93 (-0.60); RULER-128K overall 72.00 vs 72.12 (+0.12)
  setup: Table 3 details. HELMET Rerank/RAG 34.60 vs 32.50 (-2.10); ICL 70.40 vs 72.80. RULER CWE/FWE 46.35 vs 45.00; QA1/QA2 47.80 vs 46.80; VT 97.80 vs 96.80.
  quote: "After the extension stage,MSA-CPT remains close to the Full-Attention baseline."
  where: p.11, Table 3
- claim: Mechanism: a lightweight Index Branch (one index query head per KV group, one shared index key head) max-pools token scores into block scores and takes top-k blocks per GQA group. The local block is always kept. It is trained with a KL loss against the group-averaged Main Branch attention distribution, with a stop-gradient on its input and a short full-attention indexer warmup.
  number: Bk=128, k=16
  quote: "The Index Branch adds only two projection matrices to standard GQA, operates at block granularity, and makes selections independently for each GQA group."
  where: Sec 3, p.4-5
- claim: The exp-free top-k kernel beats torch.topk and TileLang radix-select.
  number: 5.1x vs torch and 3.7x vs TileLang at N=128K, k=16
  setup: H800, fp32, median of 50 post-warmup runs. Latency in us: 779 (ours) vs 3970 (torch) vs 2864 (TileLang) at 128K with 1024 blocks. At 512K with 4096 blocks and k=16: 7880 vs 33810 vs 17779 (4.3x and 2.3x).
  quote: "Table 1 shows that our specialized kernel is fastest in all tested settings, with the largest gains at the deployed setting𝑘=16."
  where: Sec 4.1, p.6-7, Table 1
- claim: KV-outer iteration gives much higher arithmetic intensity than Q-outer iteration. The FLOPs/IO ratio is about G for Q-outer and about (2/3)Bk for KV-outer. Hot KV tiles (attention sinks) are split into chunks, and partial outputs are merged by a two-phase combine with no atomics.
  number: FLOPs/IO ≈ G vs ≈ 2/3 Bk
  quote: "Since 23𝐵𝑘≫𝐺 in practice, we choose KV-outer iteration with Q gather to maximize arithmetic intensity."
  where: Sec 4.2, p.7
- claim: Ablations support the design.
  - Dynamic selection beats a FLOP-matched sliding window on agent-task perplexity (Fig 14, B.6).
  - Without KL-gradient detach, larger KL coefficients give gradient spikes and LM-loss divergence within a few hundred steps, and short-context benchmarks regress (B.3).
  - Indexer warmup improves both short-context performance and retrieval (B.4).
  - Block size 32/64/128 has limited effect. PPL is unchanged, RULER-8K is 72.5/72.8/73.8 and RULER-32K is 66.1/65.3/64.6 (Table 4, pilot model).
  - Forced sink and local selection are unnecessary (Table 5).
  - The index value head is not needed after warmup (Table 6).
  setup: 10B pilot, 16 layers, 10.53B total and 1.47B active parameters.
  quote: "Under the same sparse selection budget, the sliding-window model has higher perplexity thanMSAacross the training trajectory."
  where: App B-C, p.17-22

LIMITS
- No KV-memory or cache-size numbers, and no end-to-end serving throughput. Speedups are attention-kernel latency at 1M, GQA vs MSA. Latency at shorter lengths is only visible as plot curves.
- Quality gaps are benchmark-dependent. The paper itself says "remaining gaps are benchmark-dependent rather than concentrated in a single capability area."
- Mixed results against full attention. MSA-CPT is below Full on GSM8K (73.7 vs 76.2), HumanEval (57.9 vs 61.0) and ChartQA (71.4 vs 75.0). MSA-PT is below on BBH, MMMU and BigCodeBench. In the ablation tables RULER-32K differs by up to about 4 points (61.5 vs 65.8, Table 5), so noise across runs is plausible. No error bars are given.
- The authors name a "residual long-context retrieval gap" and propose fixing it with longer sparse training, a larger inference budget or a richer indexer. RL post-training and agentic deployment are listed as future work. The Rerank/RAG gap is -2.10 at 128K.
- The comparison is against the authors' own GQA baseline only. There are no head-to-head numbers against DSA, NSA or MoBA, only qualitative related-work text.
- Only one model family and one configuration (Bk=128, k=16, 4 KV heads) were tested at 109B.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- GQA (Ainslie et al., 2023).
- DSA (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), the closest prior work: a lightning indexer, token-level selection, one Top-k shared across all query heads, on top of MLA.
- NSA (Yuan et al., 2025) and MoBA (Lu et al., 2025), which uses large blocks and trains the indexer only through the LM gradient.
- InfLLM-V2 (Zhao et al., 2025a).
- Inference-time sparsifiers H2O (Zhang et al., 2023), SnapKV (Li et al., 2024), Quest (Tang et al., 2024), MInference (Jiang et al., 2024), FlexPrefill (Lai et al., 2025) and InfLLM (Xiao et al., 2024a).
- FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022), FlashAttention-2 (Dao, 2024), FlashDecoding (Dao et al., 2023).
- Attention sinks (Xiao et al., 2024b). Hybrid and linear attention: MiniMax 2025a,b; Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023).
- A GPT-OSS-style learnable sink was tried and dropped.

CODE: none in the paper beyond the algorithm. Algorithm 1 (p.6) is the layer-level pseudocode:
"4: I←TopK(𝑀 idx, 𝑘) // selected block indices; local block included
5: 𝑶←TopKAttn(𝑸,𝑲,𝑽,I)"
Cost model (Eq. 12): F_GQA = 2·Hq·dh·N², F_MSA = Hkv·d_idx·N² + 4·Hq·dh·N·k·Bk.

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.1): MSA overview, with the Index Branch on the left and the Main Branch on the right. It shows the whole mechanism at a glance.
- Fig 4 (p.12): FLOPs per token (28.4x at 1M), prefill latency (14.2x) and decode latency (7.6x), GQA vs MSA at 32k, 512k and 1M. This is the headline plot. It is the one to cite for the speedup curve.
- Fig 2 and 3 (p.10): matched LM-loss curves, and KL loss plus block/score recall during conversion.
- Fig 5 and 6 (p.15-16): learned selection patterns show a local diagonal, a sink column and group-specific long-range stripes.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Extraction is clean apart from math glyph garbling, and figure plots are not readable as text. The Read tool flagged NUL bytes in my saved extraction file, which is harmless. Hardware is named only as "H800" in the abstract and Table 1. Fig 4 does not state batch size or precision.
